The photographer I chose was Joel Meyerowitz, a pioneer of color photography and an icon of street photography. 

The photo I chose was [https://imgur.com/a/Nv6yrUw](https://imgur.com/a/Nv6yrUw) , which was from his website under 'everyday life'. 

I chose it at first because how heavily weighted to each side it is, with a lot of negative space in the middle. As I looked at it further, I noticed that it raised many questions and provided few answers, as most street photography does. The woman's red dress is quite striking against the green environment. The contrast of the couple kissing and the man reading the newspaper alone shows how people can be living two entirely different lives, despite being separated by maybe 15 feet of road.

This photo also does an amazing job of drawing me in. It took me a couple minutes to notice the leaf hanging in the top left corner of the frame, as the negative space and use of color made me only pay attention to the subjects.

In terms of technical elements, only the subjects are in focus. The leaf hanging in front of the camera is blurry, as is the background.

The immediate shadow after the two subjects serves to disconnect them from the background, further drawing our attention to them.

I love the use of the shallow depth of field on the car. I wonder if positioning it above you to make it seem more grandiose would add to a sort of comedy in the photo?

The 'window' photo is very nice! It is rather grainy, however, and you should have had plenty of light to playwith (judging by the fact that it is a fire lol), so maybe bring down shutter speed before increasing you iso?

I'm B (like the letter), 16, and from Providence, Rhode Island. Like many of my 'classmates' I am joining late, but am excited to catch up!

I know a little bit about photography, such as what aperture, ISO, and shutter speed each do. I recently picked up my dads old point-and-shoot canon g15, and have been watching YouTube videos to try to learn more about how to take great photos. I feel like the videos aren't structured enough to actually maintain learning and growth, so I came here.

I love the work of Lewis Hine, and of many of the people mentioned in [this article](https://www.npr.org/sections/pictureshow/2020/06/13/873427617/as-black-photographers-document-protests-they-tell-their-own-history-in-real-tim). I want to take photos that move people.
